title: Higher Education Overgrazing: Fixed Costs Are Leaving Nothing Behind
summary:
Higher Education Overgrazing: Fixed Costs Are Leaving Nothing Behind
kjohnsonbowles… Mon, 08/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

The habits and behaviors of industry negatively impact and consume higher education and students to feed their own agendas and fill their coffers, but there is no free lunch.

Byline(s)
Kathy Johnson Bowles
full_text:
Like overgrazing livestock denuding a pasture, rising fixed costs stunt institutional growth, severely damage the balance between expenses and revenue, and erode the financial equilibrium important to making education affordable. Rising costs to do business outpace revenue (primarily tuition, fees and room and board). Utilities, insurance, food services, maintenance and construction represent major expenses in the budgets of all residential colleges and universities. These costs are not controlled writ large by the institution.

For example, U.S. institutional electricity rates tracked closely with residential rates, which increased 30 to 35 percent from 2014 to 2024 according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Electric Power Annual 2024. Along with price volatility (particularly during 2021–2023), it created significant budget pressures at higher education institutions. KFF’s annual Employer Health Benefits Survey reports health insurance premiums for employer-sponsored coverage have increased approximately 50 to 60 percent over the past decade. For colleges and universities, some health plan premiums have risen more steeply.

Property and casualty insurance for higher education campuses has also increased sharply since 2020. Insurance companies are among the largest providers of employer-sponsored group insurance to higher education institutions, and many major campuses rely on insurance for student health plans, property and coverage, and directors’ and officers’ liability. Further, food commodity prices rose sharply from 2021 to 2023, exceeding 20 percent in some categories, as reported by the U.S. International Trade Commission’s 2021 Commodity Price Surge report. University dining operations saw a 15 to 25 percent cost increase from 2021 to 2023 according to the National Association of College and University Food Services.

Meanwhile, the profits and revenue of these industries tell the story of enormous prosperity. According to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ U.S. Health Insurance Industry 2024 Annual Results and its U.S. Life and A & H Insurance Industry 2024 Annual Results, property and casualty insurers wrote $463 billion in premiums in the first half of 2024 alone, up 11 percent from the same period in 2023. Verisk and the American Property Casualty Insurance Association reported estimated gains of $95 billion for the U.S. insurance industry in the first half of 2024, as reported by Insurance Business magazine reporter Kenneth Araullo in a September 2024 article. Adjusting for over $50 billion in capital gains realized by a single insurer, the estimated industry gains for the first half of 2024 were approximately $45 billion.

The construction sector physically builds higher education—campus construction and renovation represent a major segment of institutional capital spending. While construction costs have increased, U.S. construction corporate pretax profits reached $197.4 billion in 2024, up from $170.6 billion in 2023 and $165.1 billion in 2022, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis by Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Corporate Profits Before/After Tax: Construction. While some major construction firms (e.g., Turner Construction, Gilbane, Skanska) develop ongoing relationships with engineering, architecture and construction management programs at universities, their impact is mostly felt by large research and technical institutions, is not widespread in the sector, and doesn’t offset actual construction, maintenance or general operations in any significant manner.

In the near term (particularly 2020 to 2024), utilities, health insurance and food costs have risen faster than published tuition increases at nonprofit colleges and universities. From 2014 to 2024, average tuition and fees at public four-year colleges increased approximately 27 percent (see National Center for Education Statistics Table 330-10). In inflation-adjusted (real) terms, average tuition and fees decreased by approximately 11 percent between the 2019–20 and 2024–25 academic years, due to tuition freezes and increases below the Consumer Price Index, notes the College Board.

The College Board’s 2024 Pricing and Student Aid Report showed that average published tuition and fees increased less than the rate of general inflation for 2022–23 and 2023–24. Tuition increases have been restrained by enrollment pressures, political constraints and tuition freezes across more than 20 states. This is creating a major financial challenge for institutions, as operating costs are inflating faster than the primary source of revenue.

The response to the rising cost of doing business in higher education is frequently met with accusations about the sticker price of education: What happened to all the money collected through tuition, room and board? But the fact is that not all students (and in some cases, not even a majority) pay the full price. In 2020, the National Association of College and University Business Officers surveyed 361 private, nonprofit colleges and universities and found that tuition was discounted an average of 53.9 percent for first-time, full-time, first-year students in 2020–21. Meaning: A tuition sticker price of $50,000 is an average of $26,950 per student after discounts (scholarships). The purpose of a discount rate is to net the budgeted revenue and yield the number of students an institution can accommodate and make sure each student is willing and able to continue for all four years.

Institutional scholarships reduce tuition costs (or discount them) to varying degrees. Some students pay full price because they can afford it and really want to attend. Some students who can pay full price and are highly qualified may receive a scholarship as an incentive, since they have other choices. For students seeking assistance, financial aid packages are created to increase the likelihood that students will accept the offer. Scholarships come from various sources: restricted donor funds that may be used only for scholarships and budgeted institutional scholarships, often called unfunded scholarships, which do not include state and federal grants, federal loans or private loans. (More information about understanding discount rates here.)

Higher education doesn’t benefit from increasing costs to students, nor do institutions control fixed costs that make rising tuition and room and board necessary—the government and industries do. Like overgrazing, rising fixed costs, declining governmental support for controlling and funding fixed costs, and a lack of public information about higher education’s fragile ecosystem are eroding higher education’s position in society, akin to the Dust Bowl of the Great Depression.

Reporter Josh Moody for Inside Higher Ed explained, in his 2024 article “Report Finds the Higher Ed Sector Shrank by 2%,” the alarming rate of closures: “Data shared separately with Inside Higher Ed by the U.S. Department of Education show that 161 institutions either closed, merged, or otherwise lost Title IV status.”

What the Dust Bowl taught us is that unchecked expansion and greed lead to disastrous consequences. To mitigate the possibility of it happening again, the nation and the government developed a multipronged approach that led to the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Great Plains Shelter project and federal environmental policies. As a nation, are we willing to devastate the engine that drives democracy and economic success—higher education—in service of the utilities, insurance, food and construction industries’ profits? Higher education leaders, the public and legislators must say, “Hell, no.”

title: ‘AI Literacy’
summary:
‘AI Literacy’
Sara Brady Mon, 08/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

To understand a technology, you need to know the problem it was meant to solve.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
What, exactly, is AI literacy in 2026?

I ask because I keep seeing articles saying that employers want it, but I’d have a hard time saying what it is.

There’s the ability to feed data, whether numerical or prose, into an AI engine and ask it to find patterns. Then there’s the ability to identify hallucinations or errors in its output. Some would argue that awareness of the ecological impact of AI is a key part of the equation. On a more macro level, there’s legitimate concern about the impact of AI on our information ecosystem. What happens when AI engines start feeding on their own output? Veterans of the postmodernist wave will recognize that LLM’s treat language as a series of floating signifiers; it knows which words tend to go together, but it has no referent for any of them.

Worse, what happens when knowledge workers are replaced by AI altogether? (I think of that last possibility as analogous to the “recirculate” cycle in air-conditioning. It’s okay for a little while, but at some point, you need fresh air.) This is the death of the author foretold by the postmodernists, though not quite in the way they meant.

A few months ago, someone mentioned on Bluesky that to understand a technology, you need to know the problem it was meant to solve. AI is being used to solve for wages. It’s meant to do to knowledge work what automation did to manual work, with similar impact on employment.

But I don’t think that’s the AI literacy that employers have in mind.

From an academic integrity perspective, I have a concern that relatively advanced fluency in AI will result in much less fluency in literally anything else. Pushing through the friction of learning both builds skill and helps information stick; when information is handed to you on a platter, you don’t develop either the skill of learning or the knowledge base of information sinking in. Someone who’s good at using AI to fake knowledge in, say, a physics class, may come out knowing almost nothing about physics. That’s particularly true with agentic AI—bots—that can take entire online classes without the student even needing to bother feeding in prompts.

All of that said, I don’t think that channeling William F. Buckley’s famous posture—“Standing athwart history, yelling STOP!”—is an option. We need to prepare students for the world that exists and, to the extent possible, for the world that’s going to exist. Preparing them for the ’90s wouldn’t serve them at all.

In theory, I could imagine using AI for an almost Socratic form of model building. But the technology is moving so quickly that what might look like a useful approach now could be superseded in a few months, let alone a few years.

The obvious piece is error-checking. But in practice, that usually requires relatively broad and deep subject-matter knowledge, which is precisely what AI tends to prevent in people who don’t already have it.

title: Student Support Under One Roof
summary:
Student Support Under One Roof
Joshua.Bay Mon, 08/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

Temple University’s new hub centralizes essential needs resources to reduce the navigation burden and stigma students can face seeking help.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges and universities offer a wide range of resources designed to help students succeed, but having those supports available doesn’t necessarily mean students know where to find them. For students juggling food insecurity, housing challenges, financial strain or other gaps in basic needs, navigating a web of campus offices can be another barrier to getting help.

Some institutions are trying to eliminate that navigation burden by making it dramatically easier for students to get help. Temple University is betting that one way to do that is by putting all essential needs support under one roof.

The public university in Philadelphia last week opened the Christopher and Julie Barnett Essential Needs Hub, a centralized 26,000-square-foot space that offers students new and expanded resources addressing food and housing insecurity, transportation, clothing, mental and physical health, financial aid, technology access, and other needs.

John Fry, president of Temple, said the hub’s prominent location in the university’s student center was intentional, both to make resources easier to find and to normalize seeking support.

“It’s a space that conveys respect, dignity, access and welcoming, and it’s not something hidden away in a corner somewhere where people have to go find it,” Fry said. “It’s right there. It’s out front, and I think the message is that ‘Look, everyone has challenges and struggles. Come here, and this is a community that will serve you.’”

Fry said philanthropy played a significant role in supporting the hub, with donors motivated by improving the student experience. The space is named for university trustee Christopher Barnett and his wife, Julie, in recognition of their generosity to Temple.

“The philanthropy behind this has also been very meaningful,” Fry said. “Not only the amount, which has been significant, but also the intent of the donors who understand these issues and really were motivated by, ‘How do we help Temple students have the most successful experience possible?’”

The essential needs hub: Jodi Bailey Accavallo, vice president of student affairs, said the university conducted more than 100 interviews with students, faculty and staff to help inform the design of the hub. That process found that 65 percent of Temple students reported being unaware of available support services.

“Students don’t experience a university by department. They don’t know who to ask for specifically when they have a problem. They go because they have a problem, and then they need somebody to solve it,” Accavallo said. “We wanted to create a place for students to be able to start. That no matter where you come in, you’re going to get the help you need, and we will be able to do that for you.”

The initiative comes as basic-needs insecurity remains widespread among college students nationwide. A 2024 survey from Temple’s Hope Center for Student Basic Needs found that more than half of students nationally experienced at least one form of food or housing insecurity.

Reducing the stigma associated with seeking help was also central to Temple’s approach. Accavallo noted that even the name of the hub was intentional.

“We used the word ‘essential’ versus ‘basic’ for our needs, because if you don’t eat, you don’t sleep and you can’t get here, then nothing else matters,” Accavallo said. “Those are essential. We know that based on a hierarchy of need and all of the different social determinant models.”

One of the hub’s most significant expansions is the Cherry Pantry, Temple’s on-campus food pantry, which now occupies 3,000 square feet and provides students with free nutritious food and personal care products. The larger space allows for additional food storage, more frequent deliveries and a more consistent supply of fresh produce. It also houses a SPOT Period Satellite Menstrual Hub, offering free period products to the university community.

The expansion comes after the original pantry served more than 800 students per week last year, Accavallo said.

“Our students responded to it resoundingly. And so from there, we said, ‘OK, what else can we do?’ And the way that the Essential Needs Hub is set up actually now is very much like an IKEA,” Accavallo said. “So if you’re starting to think about the fact that you have food insecurity, from there, you actually exit out through the hub itself, so that there are other services that you walk through, and it might trigger, ‘Oh, I do need to talk to this person, or I would like that other service as well.’”

Other resources in the hub address needs beyond food insecurity. Temple Thrift provides students with affordable clothing, shoes and other essentials, as well as free graduation regalia. Dedicated health and well-being spaces offer resources for emotional wellness, relaxation, mindfulness, self-care and sensory needs.

But the hub is also designed to serve as a gateway to resources across the university. From there, students can be connected with services addressing financial aid, mental and physical health, housing, crisis support, and other needs.

Removing the friction: The hub employs about 20 student workers, who receive training in trauma-informed intake through Temple’s health center and residence life teams, Accavallo said. The training is intended to ensure students can ask for assistance without feeling stigmatized when they enter the space.

“Everybody matters in that space, and that’s why it’s not just a food pantry, it’s not just a place to get clothing, but you can ask questions in a variety of different ways,” Accavallo said. “The ethos of care matters and giving every person dignity matters because we’ve all had to have help one way or another.”

Accavallo said Temple plans to track student retention and persistence as measures of whether the hub is helping students access the support they need to, ultimately, stay enrolled.

Accavallo said Fry’s emphasis on student success as an institutional priority has also shaped the university’s approach to the hub.

“One of the things that he said to me is ‘Jodi, find the friction and remove it. Move quickly, move thoughtfully, and get our students to where they need to go,’ and that’s really why we’ve been able to move forward,” Accavallo said.

title: University of Houston Cuts 40% of Core Courses
summary:
University of Houston Cuts 40% of Core Courses
Ryan Quinn Mon, 08/24/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
The University of Houston System Board of Regents has approved removing about 40 percent of the courses that counted toward its flagship institution’s core curriculum requirements. The system says these courses will still be offered, but won't meet general education requirements.

The Houston Chronicle, which reported earlier on the vote, said it obtained a list of the roughly 100 cut courses, which include Black Liberation Theology, Intro to Global Climate Change, Intro to Ethnic Studies, Intro to LGBT Studies, Intro to Women’s Studies, the Bible and Modern Pop Culture, the History of Jewish Food, Dante and His World, Greek and Roman Myths of Heroes, Entrepreneurship, Tourism, Business Law and Ethics, and more. The University of Houston's American Association of University Professors chapter provided Inside Higher Ed the same list, though the university and system spokespeople didn’t confirm or deny it.

The system did confirm that the changes, which the board approved unanimously Thursday, drop the number of core courses students can choose from 241 to 144. The changes affect first-time students starting this fall. Many diversity-related courses will still count toward the core, including Intro to African American Studies, Introduction to Mexican American Studies and Latina/o Jewish History.

Texas Republican lawmakers passed Senate Bill 37 last year. A law that, among other things, requires public universities’ governing boards to review general education curricula every five years. The new law is part of a trend of red-state legislatures getting involved in gen ed.

SB 37 says the review must ensure the required courses are “necessary to prepare students for civic and professional life,” among other such broad, undefined criteria. The board’s vote Thursday was couched as part of the SB 37 review, but the University of Houston AAUP chapter has argued administrators are reading the law wrong.

In a July letter to university administrators and the Core Curriculum Working Group, the chapter wrote that administrators are “interpreting SB37 expansively in ways that go well beyond what the statute’s text requires.” The chapter further wrote that “there is virtually no transparency in this process. The committee’s report fails to identify which specific SB37 criterion is being relied on to justify the removal of any given course.”

David Mazella, an AAUP member and tenured associate professor in the University of Houston English department, told Inside Higher Ed the administrators are “aggressively complying with what they think are the requirements.”

“If those courses do not satisfy core requirements, they may go away, because we’re also under enrollment pressures," Mazella said. He called the overall situation the “Orbanization of higher ed in Texas,” referring to the ousted Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who cracked down on universities during his time in office.

title: Manifest Global acquires EduGo Abroad to expand Europe offering
summary:
Singapore-headquartered Manifest Global has acquired India-based international education consultancy EduGo Abroad, in a move that will strengthen the group’s presence in the European higher education market.

The post Manifest Global acquires EduGo Abroad to expand Europe offering appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
EduGo Abroad will join Manifest’s portfolio of international education businesses, which includes Cialfo, BridgeU, Kaaiser and Explore.

The company said the acquisition adds a “dedicated Europe corridor” to its platform and will expand its reach among students, universities and recruitment partners globally.

Speaking exclusively to The PIE News, Manifest’s CEO, Rohan Pasari, said the top countries that EduGo serves are France, Spain, Germany, Italy and Ireland. “It’s a genuinely diversified European footprint rather than a bet on one or two markets, which is part of what makes the corridor valuable,” Pasari told The PIE.

The company said that the move comes at a time when Europe is “increasingly moving from an alternative study destination to a first-choice corridor for internationally mobile students” and said that “with active policy support for student mobility across the region, Europe has become one of the world’s most connected higher education markets”.

Founded in 2009 by brothers Chintan and Bhargav Modi, EduGo Abroad has developed partnerships with more than 280 universities and colleges across 18 European countries. The company has supported almost 10,000 students to date and works with a network of channel partners across India and the wider region.

Pasari added that EduGo is “growing rapidly”, and now placing around 1,000 students per year. “That growth tracks Europe’s shift from an alternative destination to a first choice for Indian students,” he said, adding that the company is well-known in western India – its “core market”.

Through the acquisition, students using Manifest’s platforms will be able to consider European study destinations alongside the other markets served by the group.

EduGo’s university partners will also gain access to Manifest’s international student network and its technology for student recruitment and enrolment.

“EduGo Abroad built its position in Europe before the market moved there,” said Pasari. “Our approach is to back operators who know their corridor better than anyone else, and to give them AI and reach they could not build alone. Chintan, Bhargav, and their team are those operators.”

Our approach is to back operators who know their corridor better than anyone else, and to give them AI and reach they could not build alone

Rohan Pasari, Manifest

Chintan Modi, managing director of EduGo Abroad, said the acquisition would give the company’s partners access to a wider range of destinations and Manifest’s technology.

“In Manifest Global we have found a powerful new home for EduGo Abroad and for the partners who have grown with us,” he said.

“Our partners get more destinations and Manifest’s transformative AI technology. Our universities get access to students well beyond India. For everyone who has grown with EduGo, the ambition just got larger.”

The acquisition forms part of Manifest’s wider strategy of bringing together regional education specialists and technology to support international student mobility.

Pasari told The PIE that Manifest was attracted to EduGo – which will keep its name as well as its leadership following the acquisition – due to the expertise demonstrated by the Modi brothers.

“Chintan and Bhargav backed Europe as a serious destination years before the rest of the market moved there, and built real depth,” he said. The company was also impressed by the “quality of the operators”.

“This is a business built on trust with students and partners, and that is genuinely hard to replicate. We back operators who know their corridor better than anyone, and they are exactly that,” he said.

Manifest describes itself as building an AI platform for “global human capital mobility”, spanning student recruitment, talent development and cross-border movement.

The group said more than 80,000 students who choose to study outside their home country each year use platforms across its portfolio, while its university network spans more than 150 countries.

title: From Classroom to College: Practices That Help Students Succeed in Both K-12 and Higher Education
summary:
One year ago, I was greeting my 30 third graders. Students came into the classroom with crayon colored artwork, miscellaneous items found outside, and were excited to tell me about their stories from yesterday and the fun video games they played last night. Now I stand as a college instructor teaching 19 undergraduate students from college freshman to seniors ready to […]

The post From Classroom to College: Practices That Help Students Succeed in Both K-12 and Higher Education appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
One year ago, I was greeting my 30 third graders. Students came into the classroom with crayon colored artwork, miscellaneous items found outside, and were excited to tell me about their stories from yesterday and the fun video games they played last night. Now I stand as a college instructor teaching 19 undergraduate students from college freshman to seniors ready to graduate. They come into my morning class with air pods in, coffee in hand, and exhausted from late night intramural games and sorority events.

Regardless of the age of students, I am charged with the same task, to inspire and motivate students to love learning and live transformed. Throughout education preparatory classes, future teachers are taught techniques to motivate, engage, and form their students as they teach material. Transitioning into this new university instructor role, I see how the kindergarten through high school (K-12) teacher training has helped increase engagement, connection, and learning in the college classroom environment. The high-quality teaching practices are not just confined into the elementary, middle, and high school spheres of teaching. College professors should consider the same essential techniques that teachers use in the K-12 setting to engage students and build a classroom community. While college students may be more mature and have more autonomy, the teaching quality and techniques translate seamlessly into the college sector.

Using research and personal experience, I present three key practices that shape K-12 teaching which are also essential for higher education professors and their students. Professors must develop relationships, expect and create engagement, and use explicit instruction. As we unpack each of these strategies for effective teaching and classroom culture, there will be easily transferable ideas to implement into every college class regardless of content or size.

1. Build Relationships That Create Belonging

To begin, any K-12 educator knows relationships are essential to learning (Speakman-Spickard, 2019). Professors then need to lead out in caring for students, letting them know they are valued, and creating an atmosphere of belonging. Pamela Ertel (2014) shares from the ABC’s of Classroom Management that within the K-12 classroom, teachers greeting students at the door creates a culture of care for students. In addition, knowing each student by name (Miller, 2024) and creating morning meetings (Kriete, 2002) or moments for students to connect transforms the classroom environment. Even in the college setting, students need to feel welcomed into the learning space. As I taught, I tried to embody the role of hospitality for college students especially needed in the windowless basement room where our leadership class met. Enthusiasm and joy were the decorations I brought into the space. Regardless of the classroom setting, professors can set the tone of welcome and excitement even without colorful and motivating decorations like those that once filled my former third grade classroom. Therefore, I greeted each college student at the door before class and then rotated the role for students to welcome their peers each day at least five minutes before class began.

As James Lang (2016) writes,“emotions capture the attention of our students” while also focusing on “the immense power that personal connections and relationships have on the total college experience for students, including the learning that takes place in the classroom” (pp. 173, 177). Coming early to class and greeting students can help build and form relationships as the professor gets to hear their stories, frustrations, and see each student (Eng, 2017, pp. 34,101). The additional time it takes to welcome students, engage in a class question, or partner dialogue helps build relationships and encourage students to be more involved in the class. When students are seen, they begin to share more and a sense of community connects the class together.

Often professors do not prioritize building relationships but focus more on the content. Seeing students as people is essential before instilling the rich, learning material. Susan Blum (2024) in her book Schoolishness, quotes educator Sean Michael Morris, who enhances this idea that teachers should orient “toward nurturing not just the intellect of your students but also their emotional lives. Love in pedagogical works is an orientation…it is a decision to commit first to the community of learners and second to the material we’ve come to teach” (p. 246). When we focus on building relationships, seeing the college students as whole beings, and knowing them on a personal level, our classrooms will be effective and influential. All teachers at all levels need to develop relationships with their students.

2. Create and Expect Active Engagement

When both teacher-to-student and peer-to-peer interactions occur, it helps to create effective classroom engagement. Understanding Vygotsky’s idea of social-constructivism, students learn through engaging in interactions with others. Therefore, professors need to create and expect engagement in each class. One question professors can ask each day is, “How can I get my students engaged and interacting in this lesson?” Often college students come into the class ready to be lectured at or watch a slideshow of material where they check-out. In K-12 classrooms, students have multi-modal learning with hands-on instruction, movement around the room, and pair + share opportunities with partners. Professors need to expect students to engage and create moments for them to partake in the learning using their whole selves.

In the college course, I started each day with a question to frame the class discussion. Students were able to ease into the classroom discussion through simple conversation that led to deep dialogue and debate over a variety of topics. Other class activities included acting out roles and modeling leadership scenarios. Afterwards, the students eagerly asked for more opportunities to interact and engage in these types of ways. Additionally, in order to engage college students with their whole selves, they also need to activate their learning using movement with their physical bodies in the classroom. Human continuums are a great way to get students up and thinking critically while interacting productively with their peers (Teach Britannica, 2025). The movement and discussion encourages connection, deeper learning, and brings a change to “normal” lecture style instruction.

3. Give Students the Clarity They Need to Succeed

Finally, even college students need explicit, simple instructions. Clarity is key. Undergraduate students need clear expectations beyond the written syllabus. Often there are assumptions that both professors and students have in which the lack of met expectation causes frustration. This notion was revealed in my current undergraduate class when two guest speakers came in to share. The first shared wonderful engaging points but students did not take notes. The next speaker said “write this down” and all students swiftly proceeded to take out their notebooks to diligently take notes. Each class following, I explicitly told them “take out your notes,” echoing similar instructions I would use to guide for my elementary classroom procedures.

The students needed the prompting and encouragement instead of me assuming they would automatically take notes, because students have to be trained in the expectations desired of them. Using resources like Teach like a Champion helps in giving practical tools and strategies to support teaching and student learning (Lemov, 2021). From teaching third grade to teaching college, students need clear, explicit instructions which embody techniques useful for all ages.

Therefore, from kindergarten to the college seniors, and from hand drawn pictures and playground stories to airpods and coffee mugs, the simple teaching techniques that engage rug time stories also help to capture tuned out college students. All students desire to belong, be known, and be given purpose. Professors need to develop relationships, expect and plan for engagement, and have explicit instructions which does not belittle their students but rather elevates the learning and connectedness in the classroom.

Meredith A. Frey, MA, is a current PhD student in P-12 Educational Leadership at Baylor University and teaching an undergraduate course on Leadership. She completed her undergraduate studies at Wheaton College in Elementary Education with a minor in Urban Studies. While receiving her master’s in Educational Leadership, she taught elementary at a classical school in Texas and was a fellow with the Baylor Center for School Leadership. Outside of researching global education, AI in schools, outdoor education, and creating thriving learning communities within schools, Meredith loves connecting with people over coffee conversations and being active through run clubs, pickleball, and traveling.

References

title: Climate marketing: come la bolla di calore cambia i brand
summary:
Il cambiamento climatico entra nelle strategie dei brand: dal minimalismo visivo ai piani termosensibili, fino al ruolo dei dipendenti come ambasciatori, il marketing cerca nuove risposte alla pressione del caldo, dei consumi e del sovraccarico informativo

L'articolo Climate marketing: come la bolla di calore cambia i brand proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
L’ondata di caldo mai registrata in Europa, e quindi anche in Italia, porta il tema del clima nei mercati. Per la BCE possiamo parlare di climateflaction, l’inflazione provocata dal cambiamento climatico, e che potrebbe aggiungere più di un punto percentuale ogni anno fino al 2035.

Nel 2007 John Grant con il suo The green marketing manifesto aveva introdotto il concetto di marketing sostenibile capace di raggiungere gli obiettivi ecologici. Un anno fa sulla prestigiosa rivista accademica Journal of Business Research gli studiosi Sören e Sara Köcher, Linda Alkire, Susan Myrden e Genevieve E. O’Connor hanno teorizzato su come i consumatori investono risorse cognitive, emotive e comportamentali in risposta al cambiamento climatico nelle situazioni di consumo. Potremmo, quasi, iniziare a parlare di climate marketing, con il clima che spinge il marketing a cambiare sé stesso.

Climate marketing, dal green alla vita quotidiana

Se per anni i marketer hanno impostato strategie e campagne sul racconto di come salvare il Pianeta, oggi il focus è la quotidianità che cambia. L’ondata di caldo ha portato il tema clima fuori dalla nicchia degli ecologisti e lo ha reso mainstream.

Marco Gisotti, giornalista e divulgatore esperto di green economy, spiega “Salvare il Pianeta è sempre stata un’espressione generalista e, di per sé, poco utile. L’emergenza termica, quale manifestazione fenomenologia del mutamento climatico, cessa di essere una proiezione scientifica futura per configurarsi come un elemento determinante dell’esperienza quotidiana delle persone. I mutamenti climatici non modificano soltanto le necessità materiali ma ridefiniscono le temporalità, le geografie e le modalità di fruizione dei servizi e dei prodotti da parte dell’utenza”.

Oggi il marketing non vende più solo prodotti green ma soluzioni per vivere meglio. Nike con la sua campagna Move to Zero declina il suo impegno ambientale a favore degli sportivi che in alcune zone degli USA potrebbero vedere ridurre il tempo trascorso in campo fino a due mesi a causa del cambiamento climatico. Il birrificio olandese Heineken ha messo il suo impegno per tutelare la qualità e la disponibilità dell’acqua del vecchio Reno, il fiume che scorre nei pressi della loro sede, che il cambiamento climatico potrebbe minacciare.

“Presto sulle etichette e nelle campagne di comunicazione non basterà scrivere ‘ non nuoce all’ambiente’ ma potremmo vedere comparire ‘non modifica il clima’” ha detto Gisotti.

“Il saggio di John Grant appartiene a un’epoca in cui la sostenibilità era vissuta come una scelta etica della singola persona, un bollino ‘verde’ da esibire per intercettare una nicchia di consumatori sensibili. Oggi, la sostenibilità diventata un bisogno fisiologico di sicurezza e di adattamento alla realtà quotidiana. Questo significa che le aziende, i brand (ma anche le pubbliche amministrazioni per i servizi di loro competenza) non possono più limitarsi a fare leva sulla colpevolizzazione o sul senso del dovere del consumatore proponendo semplicemente l’alternativa ecologica di un vecchio prodotto” spiega Chiara Bianchini, coordinatrice del tavolo ambiente e sostenibilità di Fondazione Italia Digitale tra le cui attività c’è il Triathlon Ambientale nel quale si discute sul fatto che la transizione ecologica e quella digitale debbano convergere per generare nuovi stili di vita più flessibili.

Il climate marketing nell’era della bolla di calore

Intanto la cosiddetta ‘ bolla di calore’ con temperature record, consumi energetici in crescita e infrastrutture sottoposte a uno stress senza precedenti comincia a far interrogare i marketer anche sulle strategie e le architetture marketing e comunicazione, nonché sulla tecnologia simbolo di questa fase storica: l’intelligenza artificiale. È presto per parlare (già) di cambiamento, ma alcuni segnali sono interessanti e meritano un approfondimento.

Stanchezza dei consumatori e comunicazione termosensibile

Business of Fashion la rivista anglo-americana che si occupa di moda e lusso ha parlato di un ritorno alle comunicazioni più lente, rischi creativi più ponderati e una maggiore connessione umana, mentre le aziende e i loro brand ricalibrano le proprie strategie di intrattenimento, coinvolgimento e fidelizzazione nell’era della stanchezza dei consumatori.

Quando il caldo e l’umidità da record si fanno sentire, le persone entrano nel cosiddetto cocoon stage. In sintesi: fa così caldo che il cervello delle persone fatica a concentrarsi su dettagli complessi e a prendere decisioni. Un ulteriore stress che si aggiunge ad altri tipi di stanchezze già presenti nella vita dei consumatori.

Per Chiara Bianchini la vera frontiera della comunicazione contemporanea è quella di creare piani editoriali flessibili e termosensibili, capaci di attivarsi in base alle temperature reali, e aggiunge: “servirebbe la progettazione di una comunicazione visiva defaticante. Quando il sole picchia e gli schermi dei telefoni si surriscaldano, i brand dovrebbero proporre interfacce visive riposanti, come l’uso intelligente della modalità scura o palette cromatiche fredde e decongestionanti. Inoltre, diventa fondamentale ripensare la temporalità dei servizi offrendo anche soluzioni asincrone, come promozioni dedicate esclusivamente alle ore notturne o facilitazioni per chi sceglie di interagire con il brand nei momenti di tregua dall’afa. Adattare la comunicazione al meteo diventa una forma di rispetto per il benessere psicofisico dell’utente”.

Se nell’era dell’attenzione vinceva chi riusciva ad aggiungere stimoli, funzionalità e contenuti, oggi il marketing deve, forse, iniziare a guardare a quella che potremmo definire l’economia della sottrazione. E se tutto diventa più essenziale diventa importante la fiducia. Progettare meglio, rendere un sito più veloce, un’applicazione meno energivora, un packaging più leggero, una comunicazione più immediata utilizzando l’employee advocay.

“La sottrazione, però, non significa semplicemente eliminare elementi o rendere tutto grigio. Significa creare una gerarchia più chiara e lasciare emergere pochi codici realmente riconoscibili spiega” spiega l’art director Mario Neri.

Climate marketing e intelligenza artificiale a basso impatto

La vera innovazione, dunque, in un contesto dominato dall’incertezza climatica, economica e geopolitica, non consiste nell’aggiungere nuove tecnologie, ma nel ripensare il modo in cui queste vengono utilizzate. È una prospettiva che investe direttamente anche la grande protagonista degli ultimi anni: l’intelligenza artificiale.

Negli ultimi due anni l’AI generativa è stata raccontata come la tecnologia destinata a ridefinire ogni settore economico. Le imprese hanno accelerato gli investimenti, i provider hanno aumentato la capacità di calcolo dei data center e il mercato ha iniziato a considerare la disponibilità di modelli sempre più potenti come il principale indicatore di competitività.

Come ha ricordato Benedetta Brighenti, Climate Pact Ambassador della Commissione UE secondo i dati elaborati dall’Agenzia Internazionale dell’Energia (International Energy Agency, IEA), a livello globale i data center hanno consumato l’1,5% dell’energia elettrica mondiale.

Inoltre, ha ricordato Brighenti, secondo le stime, ogni messaggio testuale consumerebbe circa 0,3 wattora, ma i consumi sono maggiori se si parla di foto e video generati.

Le ondate di calore stanno già mettendo sotto pressione reti elettriche e infrastrutture digitali. Temperature estreme, picchi di domanda elettrica e costi energetici crescenti rischiano di trasformare quella che oggi è una leva competitiva in un fattore di potenziale vulnerabilità.

Anche il marketing sarà chiamato a misurarsi con questo aspetto. Dal team AI della digital agency Ventie30 non mostrano preoccupazione, ma invitano alla responsabilità alle funzioni governance ed hanno studiato soluzioni ‘low impact’ per aziende e brand.

Minimalismo visivo e sottrazione

L’autorevole rivista tecnologica statunitense The Verge, annuncia una virata – da parte delle aziende e dei loro brand – verso il minimalismo visivo. Se l’AI promette (e mantiene) di produrre immagini infinte il vero tratto distintivo sembra essere diventato la capacità di togliere.

Ne è convinto l’art director Mario Neri “Oggi tutti possono produrre moltissimi contenuti e l’intelligenza artificiale dà spesso l’illusione che chiunque possa realizzare immagini o comunicazioni visivamente sorprendenti, anche senza una vera cultura progettuale, fotografica o artistica. Proprio per questo il valore si sta spostando dalla quantità alla capacità di scegliere, selezionare e sottrarre. Il lusso diventa pubblicare meno, usare immagini più curate, rallentare il ritmo e lasciare maggiore spazio al gesto umano”.

Reuters, una delle più grandi agenzie di stampa al mondo, ha lanciato una campagna ‘Pure news, straight from the source’ ideata dall’agenzia di innovazione creativa Gravity Road, puntando sulla sottrazione visiva come elemento per sottolineare autorevolezza ed affidabilità.

Apple negli ultimi anni ha ridotto via via la saturazione delle immagini nelle comunicazioni dei suoi prodotti puntando su colori neutri ed essenzialità. “La lezione più importante di Apple non è usare meno colore o rendere tutto bianco o grigio. È la capacità di costruire una gerarchia molto precisa. Un prodotto, una caratteristica, un gesto e un messaggio. Tutto il resto viene eliminato per non creare competizione visiva. È una strada che consiglierei alle aziende: ridurre il numero dei messaggi, scegliere un centro visivo preciso e rendere immediatamente comprensibile quello che si deve comunicare” spiega Mario Neri.

Attenzione però se i brand rinunciano all’elemento colore rischiano di perdere un potente vettore identitario, ma anche qui, nelle scelte cromatiche, l’emergenza caldo e più in generale il cambiamento climatico può incidere nelle scelte dei team marketing?

“Credo che l’emergenza caldo stia contribuendo a modificare anche la nostra sensibilità visiva” ne è convinto l’art director Mario Neri. “Quando siamo esposti a temperature elevate, affaticamento e sovraccarico digitale diventiamo probabilmente meno disponibili verso comunicazioni troppo aggressive o sature di stimoli. Per questo vedo emergere palette più controllate, immagini meno cariche, movimenti più lenti e messaggi più essenziali”.

“Non semplificherei però dicendo che il caldo porta a utilizzare meno colore. Direi che genera un bisogno più ampio di freschezza, respiro, rallentamento. La comunicazione sembra voler cercare di non surriscaldare ulteriormente lo sguardo. Se il marketing del passato cercava spesso di aumentare continuamente la temperatura emotiva, oggi alcuni brand stanno iniziando a raffreddarla, scegliendo linguaggi più umani, silenziosi e contemplativi” conclude Neri.

Climate marketing e dipendenti come ambasciatori

Nell’economia della sottrazione emerge un protagonista che fino a pochi anni fa occupava un ruolo marginale nelle strategie di comunicazione: il dipendente. Non più soltanto una risorsa interna da informare, ma un vero e proprio punto di contatto tra l’organizzazione e il suo ecosistema esterno.

È la crescita dell’employee ambassadorship, un fenomeno che sta trasformando il modo in cui le aziende costruiscono reputazione e relazione con i propri pubblici. A confermarlo il rapporto sulla comunicazione interna delle aziende italiane realizzato dal Centre for Employee Relations and Communication (CERC) dell’Università IULM di Milano nel quale si legge che il 79% delle aziende intervistate dispone di una funzione formale di comunicazione interna, perlopiù collocata in capo alla comunicazione (solo il 5% la colloca nella direzione marketing) con una crescita dell’impatto della funzione sulle decisioni strategiche. Il vantaggio, per le aziende con una funzione di comunicazione interna, secondo Alessandra Mazzei, Direttrice del CERC e professoressa di comunicazione di impresa all’Università IULM, “è accrescere l’engagement dei collaboratori, perché solo i collaboratori ingaggiati sono motivati ad agire e a comunicare in modo focalizzato e strategico rispetto agli obiettivi di business dell’azienda. Il CERC definisce questo modello evoluto di comunicazione interna ‘Modello Enabling’, cioè volto a mettere in grado manager e collaboratori di essere comunicatori strategici a favore dell’organizzazione.

Ecco l’era dell’Interest media company, non più solo informazioni, ma l’attivazione dei collaboratori ad essere elementi attivi della comunicazione.

Come, ad esempio, in occasioni di grandi cambiamenti, vedi l’ondata di caldo, “Guardando al breve periodo le aziende possono usare la comunicazione interna come leva cruciale per gestire le emergenze come questa del caldo. Esse devono infatti diffondere le misure che le aziende prendono per tutelare i collaboratori stessi in maniera tempestiva e presso l’intera popolazione aziendale. Per esempio, aziende che operano attraverso cantieri all’aria aperta possono rivedere i turni e gli orari di lavoro per evitare le ore più calde; oppure prevedere pause più frequenti per trovare ristoro al fresco e bere. Queste misure vanno comunicate in modo tempestivo e capillare e inquadrate in termini di senso perché i collaboratori le seguano con convinzione per la loro stessa sicurezza” spiega Alessandra Mazzei.

“Le aziende dotate di competenze e strutture di comunicazione interna sono quelle più pronte a realizzare con efficacia gli interventi di emergenza e si rivolgono a collaboratori più propensi ad accogliere i messaggi aziendali” conclude Mazzei.

Per decenni il branding è stato costruito prevalentemente attraverso elementi esterni: identità visiva, campagne pubblicitarie, posizionamento, storytelling. Oggi il brand diventa sempre più il risultato delle esperienze generate dalle persone che lo compongono. I dipendenti ne diventano ambasciatori e testimonial poiché portatori di una forma di comunicazione difficilmente replicabile: quella fondata sull’esperienza diretta.

Il climate marketing tra prudenza e sperimentazione

Se per i marketer più visionari possiamo già parlare di incidenza del cambiamento climatico sul marketing e sulla comunicazione c’è chi invita alla prudenza. Per Marco Gisotti “il marketing è sempre stato adattivo e conservativo, modificando appena il necessario ma senza intaccare la comfort zone del consumatore. Non credo sia possibile invertire la tendenza ad usare in modo meno continuativo – per esempio – gli smartphone, anche con il caldo estremo”. Eppure, i segnali di un cambiamento ci sono tutti. “L’autorevolezza di un brand si costruirà sulla capacità di togliere il rumore di fondo” spiega Chiara Bianchini.

Per i marketer più innovativi i mesi più caldi dell’anno possono diventare un nuovo terreno di sperimentazione di strategie nuove, strumenti pensati (anche) per il benessere, campagne che rassicurano, time table fuori dai soliti schemi, siti web a basso impatto energetico, formati light e dipendenti e collaboratori come termometro reputazionale anche fuori dall’azienda.

Senza dimenticare l’aspetto emozionale. “Stanno tornando la fotografia a pellicola, i video in VHS, il disegno a mano, i montaggi meno curati e i linguaggi visivi meno curati. I grandi brand stanno riscoprendo il valore della mano, della materia e dell’imperfezione” ha detto l’art director Mario Neri. Chiara Bianchini di Fondazione Italia Digitale richiama l’arte di far durare le cose, con prodotti duraturi, servizi di riparazione e soluzioni che offrano la salute fisica e mentale al centro.

Un richiamo alle estati di qualche anno fa, quando le spiagge erano l’arena della comunicazione e la crisi climatica non era ancora entrata nel carrello della spesa.

È una strada che consiglierei alle aziende: ridurre il numero dei messaggi, scegliere un centro visivo preciso e rendere immediatamente comprensibile quello che si deve comunicare” spiega Mario Neri.

Attenzione però se i brand rinunciano all’elemento colore rischiano di perdere un potente vettore identitario, ma anche qui, nelle scelte cromatiche, l’emergenza caldo e più in generale il cambiamento climatico può incidere nelle scelte dei team marketing?

“Credo che l’emergenza caldo stia contribuendo a modificare anche la nostra sensibilità visiva” ne è convinto l’art director Mario Neri. “Quando siamo esposti a temperature elevate, affaticamento e sovraccarico digitale diventiamo probabilmente meno disponibili verso comunicazioni troppo aggressive o sature di stimoli. Per questo vedo emergere palette più controllate, immagini meno cariche, movimenti più lenti e messaggi più essenziali”.

“Non semplificherei però dicendo che il caldo porta a utilizzare meno colore. Direi che genera un bisogno più ampio di freschezza, respiro, rallentamento. La comunicazione sembra voler cercare di non surriscaldare ulteriormente lo sguardo. Se il marketing del passato cercava spesso di aumentare continuamente la temperatura emotiva, oggi alcuni brand stanno iniziando a raffreddarla, scegliendo linguaggi più umani, silenziosi e contemplativi” conclude Neri.

Climate marketing e dipendenti come ambasciatori

Nell’economia della sottrazione emerge un protagonista che fino a pochi anni fa occupava un ruolo marginale nelle strategie di comunicazione: il dipendente. Non più soltanto una risorsa interna da informare, ma un vero e proprio punto di contatto tra l’organizzazione e il suo ecosistema esterno.

È la crescita dell’employee ambassadorship, un fenomeno che sta trasformando il modo in cui le aziende costruiscono reputazione e relazione con i propri pubblici. A confermarlo il rapporto sulla comunicazione interna delle aziende italiane realizzato dal Centre for Employee Relations and Communication (CERC) dell’Università IULM di Milano nel quale si legge che il 79% delle aziende intervistate dispone di una funzione formale di comunicazione interna, perlopiù collocata in capo alla comunicazione (solo il 5% la colloca nella direzione marketing) con una crescita dell’impatto della funzione sulle decisioni strategiche. Il vantaggio, per le aziende con una funzione di comunicazione interna, secondo Alessandra Mazzei, Direttrice del CERC e professoressa di comunicazione di impresa all’Università IULM, “è accrescere l’engagement dei collaboratori, perché solo i collaboratori ingaggiati sono motivati ad agire e a comunicare in modo focalizzato e strategico rispetto agli obiettivi di business dell’azienda. Il CERC definisce questo modello evoluto di comunicazione interna ‘Modello Enabling’, cioè volto a mettere in grado manager e collaboratori di essere comunicatori strategici a favore dell’organizzazione.

Ecco l’era dell’Interest media company, non più solo informazioni, ma l’attivazione dei collaboratori ad essere elementi attivi della comunicazione.

Come, ad esempio, in occasioni di grandi cambiamenti, vedi l’ondata di caldo, “Guardando al breve periodo le aziende possono usare la comunicazione interna come leva cruciale per gestire le emergenze come questa del caldo. Esse devono infatti diffondere le misure che le aziende prendono per tutelare i collaboratori stessi in maniera tempestiva e presso l’intera popolazione aziendale. Per esempio, aziende che operano attraverso cantieri all’aria aperta possono rivedere i turni e gli orari di lavoro per evitare le ore più calde; oppure prevedere pause più frequenti per trovare ristoro al fresco e bere. Queste misure vanno comunicate in modo tempestivo e capillare e inquadrate in termini di senso perché i collaboratori le seguano con convinzione per la loro stessa sicurezza” spiega Alessandra Mazzei.

“Le aziende dotate di competenze e strutture di comunicazione interna sono quelle più pronte a realizzare con efficacia gli interventi di emergenza e si rivolgono a collaboratori più propensi ad accogliere i messaggi aziendali” conclude Mazzei.

Per decenni il branding è stato costruito prevalentemente attraverso elementi esterni: identità visiva, campagne pubblicitarie, posizionamento, storytelling. Oggi il brand diventa sempre più il risultato delle esperienze generate dalle persone che lo compongono. I dipendenti ne diventano ambasciatori e testimonial poiché portatori di una forma di comunicazione difficilmente replicabile: quella fondata sull’esperienza diretta.

Il climate marketing tra prudenza e sperimentazione

Se per i marketer più visionari possiamo già parlare di incidenza del cambiamento climatico sul marketing e sulla comunicazione c’è chi invita alla prudenza. Per Marco Gisotti “il marketing è sempre stato adattivo e conservativo, modificando appena il necessario ma senza intaccare la comfort zone del consumatore. Non credo sia possibile invertire la tendenza ad usare in modo meno continuativo – per esempio – gli smartphone, anche con il caldo estremo”. Eppure, i segnali di un cambiamento ci sono tutti. “L’autorevolezza di un brand si costruirà sulla capacità di togliere il rumore di fondo” spiega Chiara Bianchini.

Per i marketer più innovativi i mesi più caldi dell’anno possono diventare un nuovo terreno di sperimentazione di strategie nuove, strumenti pensati (anche) per il benessere, campagne che rassicurano, time table fuori dai soliti schemi, siti web a basso impatto energetico, formati light e dipendenti e collaboratori come termometro reputazionale anche fuori dall’azienda.

Senza dimenticare l’aspetto emozionale. “Stanno tornando la fotografia a pellicola, i video in VHS, il disegno a mano, i montaggi meno curati e i linguaggi visivi meno curati. I grandi brand stanno riscoprendo il valore della mano, della materia e dell’imperfezione” ha detto l’art director Mario Neri. Chiara Bianchini di Fondazione Italia Digitale richiama l’arte di far durare le cose, con prodotti duraturi, servizi di riparazione e soluzioni che offrano la salute fisica e mentale al centro.

Un richiamo alle estati di qualche anno fa, quando le spiagge erano l’arena della comunicazione e la crisi climatica non era ancora entrata nel carrello della spesa.
